notes: Vocative 'Maa' fixes the addressee as the speaker's own mother; tum->aap forces aaogi->aayengi only. Same: a child who normally says 'tum' to her mother switches to 'aap' in front of relatives or when making a formal-sounding request.

The imperative changes (kha lo -> kha lijiye) are forced by the pronoun switch. Same: a grown child who uses 'tum' with Papa at home can coax him with the deferential 'aap ... kha lijiye' when he is sulking or unwell and skipping dinner.

'Maa, tu' is the intimate register and is widely used (not substandard); kar -> karo follows from tu -> tum. Same: tu and tum sit next to each other for a mother, and one speaker slides between them depending on mood (tu when comforting her tenderly, tum otherwise).

ambiguity_reason: 'Didi' covers both one's own elder sister and fictive elder women (seniors, neighbours, service workers), and the tu/aap gap is the widest possible, so the pair could be one sister addressed mock-formally or two different 'didis'.
notes: hai -> hain agreement is forced by tu -> aap. Unlike Maa/Papa, 'Didi' does not pin down one addressee: 'tu' strongly suggests a sibling, while 'aap' fits a sister addressed teasingly or a fictive didi, so the isolated pair does not settle it.

Vocative 'Nani' identifies one grandmother; le lo -> le lijiye is forced agreement. Same: a grandchild who is casual ('tum') with Nani uses 'aap ... lijiye' to gently insist when she refuses her medicine, or when a doctor is in the room.

Only the pronoun and auxiliary (ho -> hain) change; 'kal Delhi' is held constant. Same: families vary between tum and aap for father, and a single speaker mixes them, e.g. aap at the dinner table with grandparents present and tum on the phone.

Ergative tumne/aapne; the perfective verb 'dekha' agrees with 'result', not the pronoun, so this is a single-token change. Same: an anxious child can say either to the same father, e.g. 'aapne' said nervously when expecting a scolding over the result.
Only tumne -> aapne changes, since 'khaya' agrees with 'khana'. Same: a working adult checking on her mother by phone mixes tum and aap freely; the vocative keeps the addressee fixed.

'Chef' as a colloquial vocative works with both du (start-up or trade workplaces) and Sie; hast/haben is forced agreement. In German, du vs Sie is a fixed, negotiated relationship with a given boss rather than a mood-based switch, so the two most plausibly address different bosses in different workplaces.

Feminine 'Chefin' vocative plus kannst/können agreement; 'den Bericht bis Freitag' is held constant. An employee's T/V choice toward their boss is stable once set, so duzen vs siezen signals two different boss relationships and, in practice, two different bosses.

First name + Sie (the 'Hamburger Sie') is normal in offices. A bare first name does not pick out one person, and a speaker does not switch between du and Sie for the same Lena at one point in time, so this is most likely e.g. a friend or colleague Lena vs. a client Lena.

deine/Ihre is the only change. Helping with a house move is typically a friend's favour (du), but a neighbour or colleague one siezt is also plausible, and since German T/V is stable per relationship, the pair points to two different Thomases.

deinem/Ihrem is the only change; both are idiomatic birthday greetings. A 60-year-old boss is duzt in some companies and siezt in others, but each speaker has one fixed choice, so the pair implies different bosses (or different speaker relationships), not a switch.

dein/Ihr only; 'Urlaub in Italien' is held constant. Small talk about a holiday suits both a friend (du) and a colleague one siezt, and because the T/V choice doesn't flip for the same person, this most likely means two different people named Markus.

du hast / Sie haben is forced agreement. Colloquial 'super gemacht' with Sie is fine (e.g. a manager praising staff). The register reflects an established relationship, so the most likely reading is two different Sabines (a team-mate vs. a formally addressed colleague).

kannst/können is forced agreement. Asking for a station pickup fits a friend (du) or a driver/host one siezt (Sie), and these are distinct relationships; one speaker would not alternate for the same Jonas.

The -어/-어요 ending indexes the listener, not the referent; 엄마 stays the speaker's own mother. Same: a student tells her younger brother '엄마가 전화했어' and her homeroom teacher '엄마가 전화했어요' about the same call.
Only the sentence-final politeness ending changes; '우리 형' is constant. Same: the speaker announces the brother's wedding in banmal to a close friend and in 해요체 to a senior coworker.

Subject-honorific -시- (오셨-) is kept in both, respecting grandmother, and only listener politeness varies; banmal + -시- is normal when talking to a sibling. Same: '할머니가 오셨어' to a cousin and '할머니가 오셨어요' to a parent, about the same arrival.
샀어/샀어요 only; the plain (non-시) verb for 아빠 is normal in casual speech. Same: a teenager tells a friend in banmal and a neighbour in 해요체 that the same father bought the same car.
아파/아파요 only; the referent is an animal, so no referent honorific is involved at all. Same: the owner says '아파' to a family member and '아파요' to the vet about the same dog.

내 -> 제 co-varies with -어 -> -어요 as part of the same listener-politeness choice (humble possessive in polite speech), so I treat it as dependent rather than as an independent second difference; borderline, as '내 ... 했어요' is not strictly ungrammatical. Same: one speaker reports the same sibling's exam result to a friend and to a professor.

-시- in 오셨어요 goes with the honorific noun 아드님, so it is a dependent change. 아드님 can't be one's own son, but bare 아들 can refer to a third party's son: a hospital nurse tells the patient '아드님이 오셨어요' and a colleague '(환자) 아들이 왔어요' about the same visitor.

결혼하셨어요 follows from 따님. With no possessor, '딸이 결혼했어요' reads as a parent announcing their own daughter's wedding, and '따님' is by definition someone else's (the listener's or a respected third party's) daughter. Isolated, the marker signals a different daughter.

합격하셨어요 is forced by 아드님. A university-admission report in plain 아들 is the typical proud-parent statement about one's own son, while 아드님 is how you speak of the listener's son (e.g. when congratulating), so the default readings pick out different sons.

전화하셨어요 goes with 따님. A logistical message about a phone call is a typical third-party report: a receptionist tells the client '따님이 전화하셨어요' and tells a coworker '(고객) 딸이 전화했어요', both about the same caller.

아내 -> 부인 is a lexical swap, but it is the target feature, and -시- follows from it. Bare 아내 reads as 'my wife', while 부인 is used for someone else's wife (e.g. the listener's), so the pair most plausibly refers to two different women.

이사하셨어요 is forced by 따님; '서울로' is held constant. The plain form is the natural way to report one's own daughter's move, and the honorific form speaks about the listener's or a respected person's daughter, so the isolated readings diverge.

Adding 'ji' is optional respect and doesn't change agreement (ne + sunayi). Same: a child says 'Dadi ne kahani sunayi' to a sibling and 'Dadi ji ne...' to a teacher or guest, about the same grandmother and the same storytelling.
Only 'ji' differs. Same: in a religious context like a puja, the speaker naturally adds 'ji' when telling the pandit or relatives but drops it when chatting with cousins about the same grandmother.
Only 'ji' differs, and 'bheja' agrees with 'achaar' in both. Same: 'Nani ne achaar bheja' at home vs. 'Nani ji ne achaar bheja' to the in-laws; one maternal grandmother, one parcel.
'ji' is the only change, and 'buna' agrees with 'sweater'. Same: a child shows off the sweater to friends ('Nani ne buna') and to a teacher ('Nani ji ne buna'), about the same grandmother.
Only 'ji' differs. Many families alternate 'Dada' and 'Dada ji' for the same paternal grandfather, often within one conversation, so the respect marker gives no signal of a different referent.

Only 'ji' differs, and 'dilayi' agrees with 'cycle' (feminine) in both. Same: the grandchild says 'Nana ne cycle dilayi' to friends and 'Nana ji ne...' to their parents' guests, about one maternal grandfather and one purchase.

Surname + uncle marks a parent-generation man and surname + bhaiya an elder-sibling-generation man. In a neighbourhood, 'Gupta uncle' and 'Gupta bhaiya' are typically father and son of the same household, so one speaker would not use both for the same person when talking about who lent the car.

aunty vs didi splits by generation: 'Sharma aunty' is the mother or mother-in-law of the house and 'Sharma didi' is a daughter or daughter-in-law. When it comes to laddoos sent over, the terms pick out different women of the Sharma family.

'aaye the' (honorific plural) works with both terms, so only the address term changes. uncle vs bhaiya encodes the visitor's generation relative to the speaker, so 'Verma uncle' and 'Verma bhaiya' are most plausibly two different Vermas who visited.

Only aunty/didi differs. A speaker's fictive-kin term for a given woman is fixed by perceived generation, so the invitation comes from an older Kapoor woman in one sentence and a younger one in the other.

Only uncle/bhaiya differs. A maths tutor is either a parent-generation 'Singh uncle' or a college-age 'Singh bhaiya'. A tutor on the age boundary is conceivable, but that's no strong reason to doubt the generational signal, so these are two different tutors.

Only aunty/didi differs; 'khana bheja' is constant. Like the other surname + fictive-kin pairs, the generation term separates an older from a younger Mishra woman, so the sender is most plausibly a different person.
